content: It is defined as the amount of mass that experiences an acceleration of 1 foot per second squared (ft/s²) when subjected to a force of one pound-force (lbf). Based on this definition, the mass of one slug is approximately 32.17405 pound-mass (lbm) or 14.5939 kilograms (kg). Mathematically, this relationship can be expressed as: 1 slug = 1 (lbf·s²)/ft. The slug belongs to a specific subset of coherent units known as the gravitational foot-pound-second (FPS) system. This system is one of several specialized systems of mechanical units that were developed during the late 19th and early 20th centuries. The term slug was first introduced in 1902 by Arthur Mason Worthington (1852–1916) in his work Dynamics of Rotation. However, the unit did not gain widespread usage until several decades later. A textbook from 1928 noted that no specific name had yet been assigned to the unit of mass in this context. In earlier literature, the slug was sometimes referred to by the alternative name geepound. There are also variations of the slug that use different length units. For example, the slinch is a version of the slug based on inches rather than feet. Specifically, 1 slinch is equal to 1 (lbf·s²)/in, which is equivalent to 12 slugs. Another similar unit is the blob, which is also defined as 1 (lbf·s²)/in.
